claims.text: Chemical short-range order typically suppresses lattice thermal conductivity in concentrated refractory high-entropy alloys below 1000 K.
SRO suppresses lattice heat transport by producing diffuse antiphase boundaries that scatter phonons.
The SRO-induced suppression of thermal conductivity diminishes above 1500 K.
High-temperature thermal fluctuations disrupt SRO and reduce diffuse-antiphase-boundary density.
Phonon-phonon Umklapp scattering dominates heat transport at high temperature.
SRO-induced local chemical order creates barriers to dislocation glide and increases strength.
The influence of SRO on dislocation mechanisms becomes attenuated with increasing temperature.
Thermal-conductivity suppression is most pronounced when SRO is stable and long-range order is absent.
BCC MoNbTaW can be represented in both random-solid-solution and SRO states without long-range ordering.
The intrinsic lattice thermal conductivity of random MoNbTaW is governed by mass-disorder and phonon-phonon scattering.
Controlled annealing at 800 K can induce an equilibrium SRO state in MoNbTaW.
In MoNbTaW, SRO is relatively strong at 800 K, which is above the temperature associated with long-range-ordering transitions.
Diffuse antiphase boundaries form at interfaces between SRO domains.
Local chemical-ordering clusters create potential fluctuations that scatter phonons.
SRO-treated samples will have lower thermal conductivity than random-solid-solution samples below 1000 K.
The thermal-conductivity difference between SRO and random samples will vanish above approximately 1500 K.
The magnitude of thermal-conductivity suppression correlates with the measured SRO order parameter.
The SRO effect on thermal conductivity becomes negligible when long-range order forms.
The proposed transport effect is strongest in BCC refractory HEAs with strong SRO driving forces, such as MoNbTaW.
SRO-induced strengthening through dislocation barriers correlates with phonon-scattering intensity.
